title: Should My Child Use AI to Study for IB?
summary: Learn how to tell whether an AI study tool is teaching your IB student or completing the work, with a practical evaluation framework for parents.
body_markdown:
If you are asking, **“Should my child use AI to study for IB?”** , the answer is yes, provided the tool strengthens independent thinking instead of replacing it. Effective AI explains concepts, asks questions, gives feedback, and requires the student to apply what they learned without assistance.


The key question is **who is doing the intellectual work** . Parents should judge AI use by whether their child can explain and apply the material independently afterward.


### AI tutoring versus AI task completion


A tutoring tool creates productive effort. It may break down a concept, provide a staged hint, identify an error, or generate a similar practice question. The student still recalls knowledge, chooses methods, evaluates evidence, and writes the answer.


A task-completion tool removes that effort by producing finished essays, solving complete assignments, or rewriting coursework into polished prose the student cannot explain.


AI is teaching when it...


AI is doing the work when it...


Requests an attempt before helping


Produces a submission-ready answer immediately


Gives hints gradually


Reveals every step without participation


Explains why an answer is wrong


Replaces the student's work with polished text


Generates new practice questions


Completes current homework or coursework


Tests independent understanding


Creates dependence whenever difficulty appears


A polished output is not evidence of learning. Better evidence is that the student can answer a comparable question or explain the reasoning without AI.


### What the IB says about AI


The IB does not impose a blanket ban. Its[guidance on artificial intelligence](https://www.ibo.org/programmes/artificial-intelligence-ai-in-learning-teaching-and-assessment/) encourages students to learn how to use AI critically and ethically.


However, the[IB Academic integrity policy](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/shared-resources/pdfs/academic-integrity-policy-en.pdf) makes clear that AI-generated material is not automatically the student's own work. Material incorporated into assessed work must be identified and appropriately referenced, subject to the school's rules. The IB's[questions and concerns about AI tools](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/shared-resources/pdfs/artificial-intelligence-questions-and-concerns-en.pdf) reinforces the distinction between using AI for learning and allowing it to produce work.


The safest principle is: **AI may support learning, but it must not become the author of assessed work** . Students should consult their teacher before using it for an IA, Extended Essay, TOK task, or other assessed component.


### The TEACH test for evaluating an AI tool


Parents can evaluate any platform with five questions:


-


**Thinking comes first:** Does the tool require an attempt before providing a full explanation?


-


**Explanations are verifiable:** Does it explain why a method works and encourage checking against notes, textbooks, or reliable sources?


-


**Application follows:** Does it ask the student to solve a new question or explain the concept independently?


-


**Control remains with the child:** Does the student choose the evidence, structure, method, and final wording?


-


**Honesty and privacy are protected:** Are academic integrity rules, age requirements, data retention, and deletion procedures clear?


UNESCO's[guidance on generative AI in education](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/guidance-generative-ai-education-and-research) emphasizes human agency, age-appropriate use, educational validation, and data protection. Avoid uploading identifiable coursework to unfamiliar services. RevisionDojo publishes a[student data and AI privacy summary](https://www.revisiondojo.com/data-and-privacy) , but parents should conduct the same check for every platform.


### The two-minute independence test


After an AI-assisted session, ask your child to:


1.


Close the AI tool and notes.


2.


Explain the concept in ordinary language.


3.


Complete one similar question independently.


4.


Identify the error the AI helped correct.


5.


Explain how the answer was verified.


Successful completion suggests that AI supported learning. If the student can only display the AI response or say it “looked right,” too much of the thinking was probably outsourced.


### Warning signs of unhealthy AI use


Concern is justified when AI becomes automatic rather than occasional support. Warning signs include:


-


Homework is completed unusually quickly, but tests do not improve.


-


Writing contains vocabulary or arguments the student cannot explain.


-


Entire assignment instructions are pasted into a chatbot.


-


AI is used before any independent attempt.


-


Sources, quotations, or data cannot be verified.


-


The student cannot continue when AI is unavailable.


Requesting a complete draft and lightly rewriting it is especially risky for IB coursework. RevisionDojo's guides to[ethical AI use in IB](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/can-you-use-ai-tools-for-ib-work-without-getting-penalized-ethical-use-and-revisiondojo-guidance) and[sharing assignments with AI tools](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/is-it-safe-to-share-my-ib-assignments-with-online-ai-tools) explain why feedback and questioning are safer than generated final prose.


### Productive uses of AI for IB study


Appropriate uses include requesting simpler explanations, staged hints, syllabus-specific practice questions, retrieval quizzes, and feedback on an independently written response. AI can also help students practise oral explanations, compare methods, create revision schedules, or convert completed notes into flashcards.


RevisionDojo's[IB study features](https://www.revisiondojo.com/features) combine Jojo AI with Study Notes, Flashcards, Questionbank practice, and Mock Exams. A sound sequence is to learn the concept, attempt questions, receive feedback, and retry without support. Parents can also review its[support for IB families](https://www.revisiondojo.com/parents) , explanation of[how RevisionDojo works](https://www.revisiondojo.com/help-center/what-is-revisiondojo) , and[academic integrity guidance](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-revisiondojo-helps-you-maintain-academic-integrity-while-studying) .


### Setting sensible boundaries at home


Agree on rules before deadline pressure develops. Require a genuine first attempt, factual verification, compliance with teacher instructions, and independent final wording for assessed work.


Avoid treating every use of AI as cheating, which may encourage secrecy. Instead ask, “What did the tool help you understand?” and “Can you now solve a similar question alone?”


### Conclusion


Your child can use AI for IB when it increases explanation, practice, feedback, and independent performance. It becomes harmful when it supplies finished work or conceals weak understanding.


The TEACH test and independence test can evaluate any platform. RevisionDojo tools such as Jojo AI, Study Notes, Flashcards, Questionbank, and Mock Exams are most effective when they prepare students to work successfully without assistance.
